summary:
Six evals were run, two of which ("negative-bedrock-throttling" and "negative-load-balancer-choice") were should_trigger:false tests where both variants correctly did not fire any behavior — these are marked skipped for all other dimensions and contribute no comparative signal beyond confirming both variants correctly withheld action.

Across the four substantive evals, the trigger itself fired 100% of the time for both variants in all cases, so this dimension does not differentiate them.

Meeting the expected output was mixed and is the most notable divergence:
- hyperpod-application-xid-verdict: both variants met expected output 3/3 (high confidence) — tied.
- fsx-training-slowdown-cause: both variants met expected output 3/3 (high confidence) — tied.
- gpu-log-coverage-audit: with_skill met it 1/3, without_skill 0/3 — both weak, but with_skill slightly ahead.
- preflight-long-run-readiness: with_skill met it 3/3, without_skill 0/3 — a large gap here, and assertion-level detail confirms it: several assertions (capacity-reservation comparison, GPU logging as readiness item, individually reported checks, deep-health-check reporting) pass 3/3 for with_skill and 0/3 for without_skill, while a few (per-check keyword usage) pass for both.

Assertion-level patterns show some checks are simply not met by either variant (e.g., naming the specific log stream/log group evidence in hyperpod-application-xid-verdict "always_fails" for both, and "coverage across the whole window" always_fails in gpu-log-coverage-audit) — these look like gaps in the underlying behavior or assertion design rather than a variant weakness. Other assertions pass for both consistently (e.g., verdict keyword usage, instance ID naming, no raw account ID exposure), meaning they don't discriminate between variants. A few assertions are genuinely split (with_skill passing where without_skill fails, particularly concentrated in preflight-long-run-readiness and some in gpu-log-coverage-audit), and several are flaky (inconsistent across the 3 repeated runs) for one or both variants, especially in fsx-training-slowdown-cause and gpu-log-coverage-audit.

On aggregate assertion pass rates per eval: hyperpod tied at 77%/77%; gpu-log-coverage with_skill 62% vs without_skill 25%; fsx-training with_skill 67% vs without_skill 76%; preflight with_skill 100% vs without_skill 33%. So with_skill leads in two of four, without_skill leads in one (fsx, modestly), and they tie in one.

Quality comparisons (LLM judge, head-to-head) were only available for two evals (gpu-log-coverage-audit and preflight-long-run-readiness had all quality pairs skipped, so no signal there). Where available: hyperpod-application-xid-verdict was close (with_skill favored 4, without_skill favored 3, 2 comparable, medium confidence); fsx-training-slowdown-cause leaned toward with_skill (6 vs 4, 2 comparable, medium confidence), with root_cause_accuracy specifically favoring with_skill and impact_analysis_accuracy favoring without_skill — a genuine tradeoff rather than a clean win.

Runtime and cost consistently favor without_skill being faster and cheaper: e.g., hyperpod 1m28s/$0.74 vs 2m56s/$1.46; gpu-log-coverage 2m37s/$1.31 vs 5m28s/$2.73; preflight 1m15s/$0.63 vs 3m35s/$1.79; fsx was close (22m9s/$11.04 vs 23m3s/$11.48). Variant_b also used noticeably less context window utilization throughout. However, this efficiency needs to be weighed against without_skill's weaker expected-output and assertion pass rates in gpu-log-coverage-audit and especially preflight-long-run-readiness, where without_skill's speed comes with substantially lower correctness.

Output consistency across repeated runs was mixed and often middling for both: hyperpod was "mostly_consistent" for both (tied, score 2.67 each); fsx-training was "mostly_consistent" for with_skill (2.0) vs "inconsistent" for without_skill (1.5); preflight was "inconsistent" for both (1.67 vs 1.33); gpu-log-coverage had no consistency score for with_skill (null/not computed) and "inconsistent" for without_skill (1.67). This suggests neither variant is highly stable run-to-run, and in a couple of cases without_skill showed more variability.

Overall, the picture is a set of tradeoffs rather than a uniform pattern: without_skill is consistently faster and cheaper with a smaller context footprint, but in two of four substantive evals (especially preflight-long-run-readiness) it fell well short of with_skill on meeting expected output and per-assertion correctness. In the other two evals (hyperpod and fsx) the variants were close to tied or showed a modest edge to one side on quality/assertions, and several assertions in the fixed set are failing for both variants regardless, indicating some evaluated behaviors are unmet by either agent. Confidence in the LLM-judged assertions and quality comparisons is generally medium-to-high, but sample sizes are small (3 iterations per eval) and quality/consistency data is partially missing (skipped pairs) in two evals, so these findings should be read as indicative rather than definitive.

hyperpod-application-xid-verdict.summary:
Both variants performed identically on the trigger, expected-output match, and overall assertion pass rate: trigger fired in all 3/3 runs, expected output was met 3/3 times for each variant with high confidence, and both passed 23 of 30 assertions (77%) — the exact same aggregate score.

Looking at individual assertions, the two variants track each other almost exactly, which means none of these assertions distinguish between them:
- Five assertions always pass for both (disposition keyword, evidence-bar statement, HyperPod recovery-action reporting, verdict keyword regex, instance ID named, Xid code quoted, no raw account ID exposed).
- Two assertions always fail for both: naming the specific log group/log stream for the Xid evidence, and naming the HyperPod health-agent log stream. This looks like a shared gap in the underlying behavior (or an assertion that's hard to satisfy) rather than a difference between variants.
- One assertion ("cause labelled as proven vs. hypothesis") is flaky for both, passing 2/3 times with only medium confidence.

So per-assertion results show no variant-specific weaknesses — every pass/fail pattern is shared.

Where the variants diverge is in efficiency and qualitative judgments. Variant_b ran noticeably faster (avg 1m28s vs. 2m56s for with_skill, about half the time) and cheaper ($0.74 vs. $1.46), and used less context window (3.9% vs. 6.5%), though neither showed any compaction events. All 3 runtime-compared pairs exceeded the 30s threshold for both variants, so this doesn't reflect with_skill being an outlier — both were slow relative to that threshold, at medium confidence.

On quality, a head-to-head comparison of 3 pairs (small sample) shows a mixed picture: with_skill was favored in 4 criterion-instances, without_skill in 3, with 2 rated comparable, at only medium confidence. Breaking down by criterion, with_skill was favored more on accuracy (2 vs 1) and completeness (2 vs 1), while without_skill was favored on actionability (1 vs 0, with 2 comparable). Given the small pair count (3), these differences should be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive.

Output consistency across repeated runs was identical for both variants: "mostly_consistent" overall, with the same score (2.67) and same dimension breakdown (2 consistent, 1 mostly consistent), both at high confidence — so neither variant showed more run-to-run variability than the other.

Overall, this is a tradeoff picture: the two variants are essentially tied on correctness (expected output, assertions) and stability (consistency), but without_skill completed tasks roughly twice as fast and at about half the cost with lower context usage, while with_skill showed a slight edge in accuracy/completeness quality judgments (on a small, medium-confidence sample) and without_skill a slight edge in actionability. No dimension here decisively separates the two variants.

gpu-log-coverage-audit.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task, run 3 times (with_skill appears to have only 1 run recorded for expected_output/assertions in some cases, without_skill 3 runs), investigating diagnostic reasoning about Xid errors/kernel logging on a HyperPod/ParallelCluster-style cluster.

Trigger behavior: The behavior under test fired in all runs (3/3), so the eval scenario itself was reliably exercised for both variants.

Expected output: Neither variant reliably met the full expected output — with_skill met it in 1 of 3 runs (33%) and without_skill in 0 of 3 runs (0%). Confidence in these judgments is high and low_confidence counts are 0, so this is a fairly firm (if weak-in-absolute-terms) finding: both variants struggled to fully satisfy expectations, with with_skill doing so somewhat more often.

Per-assertion pass rates: Overall, with_skill passed 5/8 (62%) of its assertion checks and without_skill passed 6/24 (25%), but note with_skill only had 1 run's worth of assertions counted (8 total across presumably fewer trials) while without_skill had 3 runs (24 total), so the raw totals aren't directly comparable in volume — the per-assertion breakdown is more informative:
- Two assertions always failed for both variants regardless of run ("coverage established across whole window" and "exact log stream name quoted") — these behaviors were not achieved by either variant, suggesting either a genuinely hard requirement or a mismatch between the assertion and realistic outputs.
- Two assertions were passed by with_skill (1/1) but failed by without_skill in all 3 runs: reporting coverage/liveness per-node (rather than as a blanket cluster statement), and reporting which log groups were searched (including non-standard names). These are clear directional differences favoring with_skill where they were checked.
- Several assertions were "flaky" (inconsistent across runs) for without_skill (and appeared only once for with_skill, so consistency can't be assessed for with_skill on these): establishing whether kernel logging was arriving before concluding on Xid errors, distinguishing "no errors found" from "not observable," quoting a full log group path, and examining at least two compute node instance IDs. On these, with_skill's single run passed, while without_skill passed only some of its 3 runs (0-67%).

Runtime and cost: with_skill took longer on average (5m28s vs 2m37s) and cost more ($2.73 vs $1.31). Context window utilization was low for both (6.2% vs 4.1%), with no compaction needed for either.

Quality comparison: No head-to-head quality comparison could be made — all 3 pairs were skipped, so this dimension provides no evidence either way.

Output consistency: without_skill's outputs were rated "inconsistent" across repeated runs (score 1.67, with 2 dimensions "mostly consistent" and 1 "inconsistent"), based on high-confidence judgments. Variant_a has no consistency data reported (null), likely because only a single run was assessed for it, so a run-to-run stability comparison cannot be made for with_skill.

Overall, this is a thin dataset (small numbers of runs, no quality-pair comparisons, uneven run counts between variants) that limits how strong any conclusion can be. Within that caveat, with_skill passed more of the checked assertions where a direct comparison existed (including two assertions it passed while without_skill failed every time), and met the expected output somewhat more often, but took roughly twice as long and cost about twice as much as without_skill. Variant_b showed some inconsistency across repeated runs, while with_skill's consistency could not be assessed due to limited data. Two assertions failed for both variants across all runs, indicating a shared gap not attributable to either variant specifically.

fsx-training-slowdown-cause.summary:
Both variants were evaluated on the same investigation task (an RCA involving SageMaker HyperPod/FSx/GPU-related infrastructure) across 3 runs each.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired in all 3/3 runs, and both with_skill and without_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs with high confidence — this dimension shows no difference between them and doesn't discriminate.

Per-assertion pass rates: Overall, without_skill passed more assertions (16/21, 76%) than with_skill (14/21, 67%), but the picture is mixed at the individual-assertion level, and every assertion is flagged as "flaky" (inconsistent across the 3 runs for at least one variant), so these rates should be read as noisy rather than definitive:
- Two assertions favored without_skill clearly: labeling causes as proven/hypothesis explicitly (with_skill 2/3 vs without_skill 3/3) and using that label verbatim (2/3 vs 3/3); also quoting FSx/GPU percentages without rescaling (2/3 vs 3/3).
- One assertion — requiring a measured saturation signal before calling something root cause — failed for both variants most of the time (with_skill 0/3, without_skill 1/3), indicating this behavior is weak or the assertion itself may be very strict for both systems.
- One assertion (naming the specific confirming measurement) tied exactly (2/3 vs 2/3).
- Two assertions favored with_skill: reporting unreadable signals as "not observable" rather than zero/healthy (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 2/3), and identifying the FSx file system (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 2/3).
So without_skill leads on more assertions, but with_skill leads on two, including one with a fairly concrete, checkable behavior (correct FSx identification).

Quality comparison (LLM judge, 3 pairs, medium confidence): Aggregated across criteria, with_skill was favored in 6 comparisons, without_skill in 4, with 2 rated comparable. Breaking this down by criterion shows a more nuanced pattern: without_skill was favored more on impact_analysis_accuracy (2 vs 1), with_skill was favored more on root_cause_accuracy (2 vs 0, 1 comparable) and key_findings_accuracy (2 vs 1), and supporting_evidence_quality was split evenly (1 vs 1, 1 comparable). With only 3 pairs evaluated, this comparison carries limited statistical weight despite the directional lean toward with_skill on the aggregate.

Runtime and cost: The two variants were very close — with_skill averaged 23m3s and $11.48, without_skill averaged 22m9s and $11.04, a small edge for without_skill in both speed and cost, unlikely to be practically meaningful on its own. Separately, a runtime-threshold check flagged 2 of 3 pairs as exceeding a 30-second threshold (medium confidence), though it's unclear which variant(s) drove this given the close averages.

Context window usage: with_skill used more context on average (67.2% utilization) than without_skill (43.7%), with neither showing any compaction events. This suggests without_skill operated with more headroom, though this alone doesn't indicate a quality difference.

Output consistency across repeated runs: with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0, all 4 measured dimensions mostly consistent), while without_skill was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.5, with 2 of 4 dimensions rated inconsistent). This is a notable difference — without_skill's outputs varied more from run to run — and should be weighed alongside its higher assertion pass rate, since higher average performance with more run-to-run variability is a different profile than with_skill's steadier but slightly lower-scoring output.

Overall, the two variants are closely matched on trigger firing, expected-output success, and cost/runtime, with no dimension showing a large, unambiguous gap. Variant_b passed more assertions in aggregate and was favored somewhat more on impact_analysis_accuracy, but with_skill was favored more on root_cause and key-findings quality criteria and showed more run-to-run consistency. All comparative quality judgments rest on only 3 evaluated pairs at medium confidence, and every assertion is flagged as flaky, so these differences should be treated as directional signals rather than firm conclusions.

root_cause_consistency.reasoning: All three iterations agree that the ultimate root cause is the loss/end of Capacity Reservation/Capacity Block cr-0013d27d3b3d5dc3b, causing RunInstances failures with 'Capacity Reservation ... is not active' and preventing GPU compute from running, ruling out storage/network. Iteration 1 frames it as 'end-of-reservation reclaim' (AWS-side expiry), while iteration 3 frames it as a launch-template misconfiguration from a CloudFormation UpdateStack on 2026-09-22 that repointed the CapacityReservationTarget to a since-deleted CR (implying human/config error rather than natural expiry). Iteration 2 does not explicitly commit to a single 'Root Cause' header at all - it lists 'no training job ran' as the primary cause and treats the capacity reservation issue as a secondary cause without labeling it definitively as the root cause, and it also doesn't explain WHY the CR became inactive (reclaim vs. config change). This is a meaningful divergence in the specific mechanism (natural expiration vs configuration change) and in whether one output even designates a clear root cause.

impact_analysis_consistency.reasoning: All three describe the same fleet (distributed-training-triage-b200, p6-b200.48xlarge) and the same FSx filesystem fs-077c776983688ad76, and all identify effectively zero/near-zero GPU utilization in the relevant window with FSx idle. However, the framing of symptoms differs: iteration 1 frames it as throughput declining over 72h reaching zero at Sep 27 11:00Z; iteration 2 frames it as a report of 'slow reading from FSx' with 'no active training job in the window' at all (a different characterization - training never ran, not that it slowed); iteration 3 frames it as a general degradation over 'the last few days' matching the original request. The scope/window and even the nature of the observed symptom (gradual slowdown vs. abrupt job crash then no job at all) diverge somewhat between iteration 2 and the others.

key_findings_consistency.reasoning: Common findings across all iterations: (1) FSx storage was idle/healthy and not a bottleneck (ruled out), (2) GPU fleet fell to zero due to Capacity Reservation cr-0013d27d3b3d5dc3b becoming inactive, causing RunInstances failures. Iteration 1 additionally finds an abrupt 'hard termination' fleet stop with clean telemetry to the instant (framed as AWS reclaim). Iteration 2 uniquely adds the finding that the last Slurm job (JobId 69) crashed with SIGABRT at 2026-09-24T19:29:29Z and was never restarted - a distinct causal finding not present in iterations 1 or 3, which instead treat GPUs as idle without explaining a job crash. Iteration 3 uniquely adds the CloudFormation UpdateStack on 2026-09-22 that repointed the launch template to the dead Capacity Block - a specific config-change finding absent in iterations 1 and 2. Iteration 3 also explores network/EFA as a hypothesis (ruling it out) which iterations 1 and 2 do not substantively address. These represent moderate divergence - shared core findings but each iteration adds a materially different unique finding.

evidence_consistency.reasoning: All three cite the same FSx filesystem ID, the same Capacity Reservation ID cr-0013d27d3b3d5dc3b, the same launch template lt-025a88cbeaba7b869, and similar GPU idle percentages (~0.58% peak in iterations 2 and 3; iteration 1 doesn't give the same exact number but references GPUPowerUtilization similarly). However supporting details differ: iteration 1 emphasizes exact timestamps like 10:59:54Z simultaneous silence across two specific instance IDs; iteration 2 emphasizes JobId 69 SIGABRT at 19:29:29Z and OSS NetworkThroughputUtilization peaks of 124.7%/97.3% on Sep24; iteration 3 cites similar FSx metrics but with slightly different framing (≤0.13% vs iteration 1's ~0.04%/0.13%/0.12%) and adds the CloudFormation UpdateStack timestamp of Sep22 19:33Z (vs iteration 2's Sep23 15:52/16:15Z UpdateStack calls - a discrepancy in dates for what seems like the same event). This is a notable inconsistency: iteration 2 says UpdateStack on 09-23, iteration 3 says UpdateStack on 09-22 for what appears to be the same launch-template-repointing event. Evidence overlaps substantially but has these specific numeric/timestamp discrepancies and unique details per iteration.

root_cause_consistency.reasoning: Each iteration names a distinctly different root cause. Iteration 1: training application crash-loop (exit 127 then SIGABRT, misconfiguration/entrypoint failure), never resubmitted. Iteration 2: Capacity Block cr-0013d27d3b3d5dc3b expiry preventing GPU node launch. Iteration 3: inter-node EFA/NCCL collective-communication stall (fabric/collective path failure) causing repeated SIGABRT aborts. While all three involve GPU nodes going idle and SIGABRT/exit codes appear in both 1 and 3, iteration 1 attributes it to an application/config bug (exit 127 command-not-found), whereas iteration 3 attributes the SIGABRT specifically to an EFA/NCCL fabric stall — different underlying causal mechanisms. Iteration 2 has an entirely different root cause (capacity reservation expiry) not mentioned as root cause in the others. These are not the same underlying cause.

impact_analysis_consistency.reasoning: All three describe the same broad scope: two p6-b200.48xlarge GPU compute nodes on the distributed-training-triage-b200 cluster going idle, FSx fs-077c776983688ad76 largely idle/healthy, GPUs idle, network idle. Time windows differ slightly: iteration 1 spans 2026-09-24T02:32Z–09-27T11:00Z, iteration 2 spans 09-24T19:29Z–09-27T11:30Z, iteration 3 starts at 09-14T00:00Z (broader) and describes throughput degradation over days rather than pinpointing exact stop time in the Symptoms section. All agree job stopped progressing around 09-24 19:29Z and nodes were reclaimed ~09-27.
